summary:
TerraShift is an open-source web app that makes NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data easy to read.
Anyone can pick a place on Earth, see which NISAR products exist, open NASA’s own preview image on a map, step through dates, compare two dates, and switch between HH and HV radar polarizations, with optical imagery of the same day for context. For four areas (farming in California’s San Joaquin Valley, earthquakes on the Caracas coast and Flores Island, and a wetland pair in Brazil’s Pantanal) we processed eight real NISAR files ourselves. Every result states how far it was checked, including checks that failed. It addresses the challenge by turning complex radar observations into
maps, time controls and plain-language explanations for scientists, teachers, resource managers and the public.
details: What it does: TerraShift lets anyone explore what NASA-ISRO’s NISAR radar satellite has observed anywhere on Earth. You search a place or click the map, and the app asks NASA’s public catalog for NISAR products over it: ground-motion products (GUNW) and backscatter products (GCOV). A calendar shows when NISAR looked and how often. For every product you can open NASA’s own preview image on the map, labelled "NASA preview, not processed by TerraShift", step through dates with a slider, compare two dates from the same track, and, for backscatter, switch between HH and HV polarizations (frequencies A and B) with a short guide on how to read each. A same-day optical (MODIS) view adds context. Each product shows a four-step status: catalog record, NASA preview, processed by TerraShift, checked against independent data. Processed study areas. For four areas we downloaded and processed eight real NISAR files ourselves (six ground-motion GUNW files and two backscatter GCOV files): surface disturbance and ground motion in California’s San Joaquin Valley, and earthquake deformation on the Caracas coast and Flores Island. We compare our ground-motion maps with independent GNSS stations (Nevada Geodetic Laboratory) and USGS earthquake data. At Caracas, GNSS station CCS1 moved 466 mm between the two radar dates, confirming the scale of the M7.5 earthquake’s motion. In San Joaquin our ground-motion map differs from GNSS by 28.4 and 51.1 mm RMS, so the check failed; we show this openly and label the result not validated. The Flores pair kept almost no usable pixels after quality masking, so we mark it quality limited and do not present it as a measured result. In Brazil’s Pantanal wetland we processed a before-and-after backscatter pair (5 July and 21 October 2026, HH and HV): the scene brightened by about 4 dB (median) in both polarizations over most of its area. We report this as a provisional candidate, not a confirmed flood, because a change this large and even could be seasonal or a processing effect. We also processed quiet-period control pairs for Venezuela and Flores, to test whether the earthquake maps stand out from background change; they are not yet compared with the event maps on the site. How it works. A React + TypeScript front end (Vite, MapLibre GL, Three.js) searches NASA CMR directly in the browser, loads NASA browse images and optical tiles from NASA GIBS, and draws processed display grids prepared by a Python pipeline (h5py, NumPy, SciPy, PyProj) from NISAR GUNW files. An optional FastAPI service supports bounded discovery and jobs. The site works without a backend and is deployed with GitHub Pages and continuous testing (pytest, ruff, Vitest, Playwright). Benefits and goals. Radar sees through cloud and darkness, but its data is hard to open. TerraShift makes it accessible: no login to explore, explanations in plain language, and honest limits. Likely drivers of change (harvest, rain, earthquakes) are always shown as hypotheses, never findings. Learn pages link NASA’s StoryMaps, applications papers, UAVSAR postcards and ARSET trainings. We hope to extend it with checked backscatter change for floods, wetlands and fires, side-by-side quiet period controls for earthquakes, and more places. Tools. React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, Three.js, Python, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, PyProj, FastAPI, GitHub Actions, Playwright, Vitest, pytest. Open source under the MIT licence: https://github.com/snslighting/terrashift Honest limits. The Pantanal result is a provisional candidate, not a confirmed finding. Flores kept almost no usable pixels, so we do not present it as a measured result. The Venezuela and Flores control pairs are processed but not yet shown or compared on the site. Floods and wildfire are not yet measured, and we have short series of pairs, not a long time series. California ground motion fails the GNSS check (28.4 and 51.1 mm RMS), and Caracas is checked at one station. Ground-motion values are provisional and not independently validated
